response.query: How can quasi-experimental variation (broadband rollouts, counselor hiring waves) be exploited to identify causal effects on humanities enrollment in China?
response.answer: Quasi-experimental designs like natural experiments can exploit broadband rollouts or counselor hiring waves to identify causal effects on humanities enrollment in China by comparing affected and unaffected groups. These methods help isolate the impact of the intervention from other variables.

results.title: The Digital Backlash and the Paradoxes of Disconnection
results.content: https://doi.org/10.48335/9789188855961 PUBLISHED BY: Nordicom, University of Gothenburg Box 713 SE 405 30 Göteborg, Sweden www.nordicom.gu.se/en GRAPHIC DESIGN BY: Karin Andén The Digital Backlash and the Paradoxes of Disconnection EDITED BY: kristoffer albris, karin fast, faltin karlsen, anne kaun, stine lomborg, & trine syvertsen 4 “After the ‘culture of connectivity’ we have entered a new zeitgeist: the ‘era of digital disconnection’. https://doi.org/10.48335/9789188855961-1 CHAPTER 1 Introduction The digital backlash KRISTOFFER ALBRIS,I KARIN FAST,II FALTIN KARLSEN,III ANNE KAUN,IV STINE LOMBORG,V & TRINE SYVERTSENVI i copenhagen center for social data science and department of anthropology, university of copenhagen, denmark ii department of geography, media and communication, karlstad university, sweden; department of media and communication, university of oslo, norway iii department of communication, kristiania university college, norway iv department for media and communication studies, södertörn university, sweden v department of communication, university of copenhagen, denmark vi department of media and communication, university of oslo, norway abstract What we in this volume call the “the digital backlash” covers a range of social and cultural practices of digital disconnection, as well as critiques of the impact of digital technologies and platforms in the world today.
